result.summary: The Chorus sings in praise of Dionysus and the simple life of faith, and longs for holy places. Guards bring in the bound Dionysus, disguised as a Lydian stranger, and Pentheus mocks him, questions him, cuts his hair, takes his staff and orders him imprisoned in the stable. Dionysus warns that the god will take vengeance.

scenes.title: The Chorus sings of Dionysus
scenes.summary: The Maidens of the Chorus pray against the King's scorn, praise Dionysus as the giver of joy and peace, and long for Cyprus, Paphos and Olympus.

scenes.title: The prisoner is brought in
scenes.summary: The Soldier brings in the calm, bound Dionysus and reports that the imprisoned Maidens escaped by miracle. Pentheus orders him freed of the guards' grip and mocks his looks.
scenes.stakes: Dionysus is a captive; the Soldier fears the wonders and Pentheus's anger.

scenes.title: Pentheus questions the stranger
scenes.summary: Dionysus says he comes from Lydia and was taught his rites by the god. Pentheus scoffs and condemns him; each accuses the other of blindness.
scenes.stakes: Dionysus faces Pentheus's sentence; Pentheus risks the god's wrath through impiety.

scenes.title: Hair cut, staff taken, prison
scenes.summary: Pentheus has Dionysus's curl cut, takes his wand, binds him and sends him to the stables, threatening his followers. Dionysus warns of the god's coming vengeance.
scenes.stakes: Dionysus is bound and imprisoned; Pentheus invites divine retribution.

characters.name: Dionysus
characters.description: god of wine, disguised as a Lydian stranger and priest of his own rites

characters.name: Pentheus
characters.description: King of Thebes, hostile to the new worship

alias_notes.explanation: A cult title of Dionysus meaning roughly 'the roaring one'.
A descriptive title the Chorus uses for the god.

notable_quotes.reason: The Chorus warns that clever wisdom claiming more than human limits is not true wisdom.
Expresses the Chorus's preference for simple popular faith over elite learning.
Ironic foreshadowing: Pentheus's name suggests grief (penthos).

analysis.text: Reason and authority clash with ecstatic religion; Pentheus cannot see the god standing before him, a blindness the play punishes.
The play reflects Athenian unease about foreign cults and the limits of rationalism, written late in Euripides's life in Macedonia.

legacy.text: Pentheus's interrogation of a disguised god is a model for later stories of tyrants confronting hidden divinity.

fun_facts.text: Pentheus's name is linked by Greek wordplay to penthos, 'grief', as Dionysus hints here.

language_notes.text: "Lord of Many Voices" is an epithet for Dionysus; "sovranty" is an archaic form of sovereignty.
"Him of mortal mother born" refers to Dionysus's birth from Semele, a mortal woman, which Pentheus denies.
"Loose thy lips from out the rein" means: speak without restraint, like a horse slipping its bridle.
"Things of clay" means mortals, who were traditionally imagined as made of earth.
"I ween" is archaic for "I think" or "I suppose".
The Nile's mouths enrich Egypt's fields; the poet imagines the river flowing under the sea to Paphos, which has no rain of its own.
"Spirit of Guiding Fire" addresses Dionysus, linked with fire and the lightning at his birth.
"Wine-red cheek" suggests the flush of Dionysus, god of wine; the Soldier means his face showed no pallor of fear.
"Wreak" means carry out; "hest" is an archaic word for command or bidding.
"Withal" means besides, also; "Maids" are the Bacchic women Pentheus had imprisoned.
Bromios, "the Roaring One," is a name of Dionysus.
"Toils" are hunting nets, continuing the hunt imagery of the Soldier's report.
"Marry" is an old exclamation meaning "indeed"; "ween" in the next sentence means suppose.
Pentheus sneers that long curls show the stranger is no wrestler; athletes wore their hair short.
"Sirrah" is an archaic, contemptuous form of address to an inferior, showing Pentheus's disdain for the stranger.
Tmolus is a mountain in Lydia, in Asia Minor, near Sardis; it was associated with Dionysus's worship and its vineyards.
"Hellas" is the Greek name for Greece; "revelations" means the religious rites or mysteries being revealed.
"Oped" is "opened"; the god disclosed the rites' purpose and use to him. The word order is inverted for the verse.
Pentheus mocks the myth that Zeus fathered Dionysus, asking sarcastically whether Zeus still begets new gods in the womb.
"Whose seal was set on Semele" refers to Zeus's union with Semele, Dionysus's mother, a Theban princess killed by his lightning.
"Emblems" are the sacred objects or tokens of the rites, revealed only to initiates.
"His Elect" means those chosen and initiated into Dionysus's mysteries.
"Deftly turned again" means cleverly deflected; Pentheus says Dionysus has dodged the question with a neat twist.
"Jape" means a joke or trick; "idle" means empty. Pentheus calls the answer a meaningless quip.
"Barbary" here means the non-Greek lands, the "barbarian" world, not North Africa.
"Ween" is archaic for "think" or "suppose"; "Hellenes" means Greeks.
"Craft and rottenness" means cunning deceit and corruption; Pentheus assumes the women's night rites are a cover for immorality.
"Brazen-browed" means shameless, with a face of brass; "knave" is a rogue.
'Tis holy hair: the uncut curl is consecrated to Dionysus, so cutting it is an offence against the god.
Pentheus sneers: the god may free him only if he ever hears Dionysus's voice again among his bands (companies) of devotees. 'Saints' here means worshippers.
'Hight' is archaic for 'called' or 'named'.
'Fore-written to calamity' means the name is destined for disaster; Pentheus' name is linked to the Greek word for grief (penthos).
Tying Dionysus in the horses' stable and manger is a deliberate humiliation, treating the god like an animal.
Distaffs are spindles for spinning wool, women's work; timbrels are hand drums used in Bacchic worship.

context_notes.text: The King is Pentheus of Thebes, who opposes the worship of Dionysus and has scorned the god.
Cyprus was the island sacred to Aphrodite, said to have risen from the sea-foam; the Loves are her attendant winged spirits.
Olympus was the home of the gods; the Muses, goddesses of song and the arts, were associated with its slopes.
The miraculous escape shows the power of Dionysus, though Pentheus refuses to see it as divine.
Pentheus does not know the prisoner is Dionysus himself, disguised as a mortal priest from Lydia.
Lydia, in Asia Minor, is where Dionysus says he comes from; in the play he has led his Asian followers to Greece.
Mystery cults kept their rites secret from the uninitiated, and the impure were barred from them.
Greeks regarded non-Greeks as inferior "barbarians"; Pentheus voices this prejudice, which Dionysus overturns.
Dionysian rites were often held at night on mountains, by torchlight, which fed Pentheus's suspicions.
The staff is the thyrsus, a wand wreathed in ivy and carried by worshippers of Dionysus.
Pentheus is king of Thebes, son of Agave and Echion, one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth.

literary_notes.text: The Chorus directly addresses a divine Purity, invoking it with epithets and appealing for it to hear Pentheus's anger.
"Grape-blood" turns wine into blood, linking the god's gift with life and divine feasting.
"The world's Wise are not wise" contrasts worldly cleverness with true wisdom, a central theme of the play.
Rainless meadows and the Nile streaming beneath the waves create a vivid, dreamlike picture of abundance.
The god gives wine to all, great and humble, yet his anger falls only on those who spurn joy.
The Chorus defines itself as simple and faithful, setting popular belief against the proud skepticism of Pentheus.
The stranger is called a "wild thing" and "prey", casting the arrest as a hunt, with irony in how tame he is.
The captive comforts his captors and laughs, so the bound man seems the one in control.
Pentheus's mocking focus on appearance and women reveals his contempt, suspicion and blindness to the god before him.
Dionysus's evasive answer hides that he is a god, so his claim of no glory or disgrace is quietly ironic.
Pentheus's mocking question shows his scorn and disbelief, and marks his impiety against the god before him.
Pentheus's angry accusation reveals his suspicious, rash temper, which prepares for his downfall.
Dionysus hints that Pentheus's spiritual blindness prevents understanding; the stranger is the god himself, though Pentheus cannot see it.
Dionysus turns Pentheus's charge back on him with "Not mine; but thine," a sharp reversal of accusation.
The disguised god calmly invites punishment from a king who will soon suffer far worse at his hands.
The audience knows the stranger is the god, so Pentheus' blindness to him, and Dionysus' claim that impurity veils him, is ironic.
Seeing is set against blindness: Dionysus has true vision while his captors, and Pentheus, are blind to the truth.
The 'name fore-written to calamity' hints at Pentheus' coming ruin.
By imprisoning the stranger Pentheus believes he has beaten the god, yet he has actually bound himself to his doom.
